name: Sulfate-free shampoo
lead: Sulfate-free shampoo is a shampoo made without the sulfate surfactants most common in conventional products, chiefly sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) and sodium laureth sulfate (SLES). It uses other cleansing agents such as sodium cocoyl glutamate or sodium cocoyl isethionate [1].

People reach for it to keep hair and scalp looking and feeling better: gentler cleansing is marketed to those with sensitive or dry scalps, textured or curly hair, and colour-treated hair, where the aim is softer-looking hair, less dryness and flaking, and colour that lasts longer between salon visits [1]. Many companies sell colour-protection shampoos, some marketed as using gentle cleansers [1].

Sulfate surfactants are widely used because they foam well and trap oil and dirt [1]. SLS is a detergent that removes oils from skin and can irritate skin and eyes, with sensitivity varying between individuals [2]. Wikipedia notes that how well sulfate alternatives clean is still open to debate [1]. No published clinical trial has compared sulfate-free and sulfate-containing shampoos for appearance outcomes.

paras: Most mainstream shampoos pair a primary sulfate surfactant (SLS or SLES) with a milder co-surfactant such as cocamidopropyl betaine in water, alongside thickeners, preservatives, fragrance, conditioning agents and an acid to bring the pH to roughly 5.5.[1] Sulfate-free shampoos replace the sulfate component with other surfactants.[1]
Shampoo as a category dates in its modern commercial form to around 1900, with synthetic-surfactant formulations arriving in the 1930s.[1]
A slightly acidic pH of around 5.5 is described as helping the hair cuticle lie flat so hair looks shinier, and conditioning shampoos add silicones or polyquaternium-10 to smooth the hair [1].

SLS removes oils from skin and can irritate skin and eyes, and it may aggravate chronic skin hypersensitivity conditions such as atopic dermatitis; individual sensitivity varies.[2] Contact allergies to shampoo ingredients of many kinds are documented, and patch testing can identify them.[1]

Claims that SLS causes cancer have been described in the 2005 Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessment as a rumor not supported by evidence, with the same review advising that products left on the skin for long periods keep concentrations at or below 1 percent.[2]

Sulfate-free shampoo is presented in hair-care routines as a gentler-cleansing option for hair that looks dry, frizzy or colour-faded. It sits alongside the "no poo" movement, in which followers reduce or replace shampooing with alternatives such as conditioner-only washing; Wikipedia notes one dermatologist's view that gradually reducing washing frequency may reduce scalp greasiness, since daily shampooing removes sebum [1]. A T Nation member who describes herself as a long-hair enthusiast refers to typical sulfate cleansers as what most people use, in a thread about hair softness and conditioner [3].

card.summary: Shampoo made without SLS/SLES sulfates; marketed as gentler, with no trials on appearance outcomes.
card.note: Cleaning power of sulfate alternatives is described as debated; no head-to-head appearance trials found.

quick.overview:
Sulfate-free shampoos leave out the common foaming detergents SLS and SLES and use other cleansers instead. They are marketed to people with sensitive scalps, dry or textured hair, or chemically treated hair.

Encyclopedic sources describe SLS as an irritant for some people but report no evidence of cancer risk at normal use. No clinical studies comparing sulfate and sulfate-free shampoos for hair appearance were found.
quick.mechanism: Shampoos clean by surfactants binding oil and dirt so they rinse away. Sulfate surfactants do this strongly and foam well; alternatives such as cocoyl glutamate or isethionate clean by the same principle, with the trade-offs in cleaning strength and foam that sources describe as debated.
quick.risks: Sulfate-free shampoos are ordinary cosmetics; contact allergy to any shampoo ingredient is possible. SLS can irritate skin and eyes in some people. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by regulators like the US FDA.

chain: Strips less scalp oil and may irritate less
Softer-feeling hair, calmer scalp, colour that people hope lasts longer
angle.text: People choose sulfate-free shampoo to clean hair with a milder detergent, aiming for softer, less dry-looking hair and less scalp irritation. It is especially associated with dry, textured or colour-treated hair.
